outcomes.original: Filing step: Confirm in writing with Planning whether the change from limited restaurant to restaurant requires Conditional Use Authorization or qualifies as continuation under Section 841. What to say: Submit a zoning question to the SF Planning information desk or request a pre-application meeting, stating: '921 Folsom St, converting from limited restaurant to restaurant (full cooking, no alcohol, closing before midnight, not formula retail if independent). Does the Youth and Family SUD require CUA for this change, or is it approved as continuation of non-abandoned restaurant use under Section 841?' Attach a one-page concept summary, floor plan sketch and photos. Do not file a CUA application or pay fees until you have the answer in writing, because if it is continuation the path is a simple agency referral.
outcomes.note: The records do not mention Section 841, continuation provisions, CUA requirements, or the agency referral path.

outcomes.original: Filing step: If Planning confirms CUA is required, file a Conditional Use Authorization application with the Planning Department, paying the application fee (about $3,100 for a use change with no new construction, subject to fee waiver programs). What to say: Frame the application as an independent neighborhood restaurant upgrading cooking capabilities to serve the established SoMa food corridor, with no alcohol service, no late hours and a Good Neighbor Policy. Emphasize that 915-917 Folsom next door operate as restaurants with alcohol licenses, and that this concept is less intensive. Include a letter of support from the property owner, renderings of the interior, a sample menu, hours of operation (e.g., 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily) and a Good Neighbor Policy draft covering trash, noise, deliveries and a contact for complaints. The CUA will be scheduled for a Planning Commission hearing 3-6 months after filing, with 300-foot mailed notice and posted notice 30 days before the hearing.
outcomes.note: The records show CUA applications exist but do not state the fee amount, hearing timeline, notice requirements, or facts about neighboring properties.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Register the business entity with the California Secretary of State (LLC or corporation, $70-$150) and obtain a federal EIN from the IRS (free, same day online). What to say: File Articles of Organization for an LLC or Articles of Incorporation online at bizfile.sos.ca.gov, then apply for an EIN at irs.gov/EIN. The entity name and EIN are needed for the San Francisco business registration, bank account, lease signature and every other permit application.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Register for a San Francisco Business Registration Certificate with the Office of the Treasurer & Tax Collector ($55-$700 tiered by gross receipts, plus $4 state fee). What to say: Apply online at sftreasurer.org/business with the entity name, EIN, lease or location confirmation and principal officer information. The Business Account Number (BAN) issued is required for every City permit (health, building, sign, DBA). If the business is in a Priority Equity Geography (the address is inside that SUD), ask whether fee waivers under the First Year Free program apply.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Submit building permit plans for tenant improvements and kitchen installation to the Department of Building Inspection, with architecture and MEP sheets routed to Planning, DPH, Fire and SFPUC. What to say: Hire a licensed architect experienced in San Francisco restaurant build-outs to prepare plans showing the kitchen layout, hood and suppression system, grease interceptor, restrooms, hand sinks, ADA path of travel and finishes. Submit the DPH health plan check application at the same time the building permit is filed, listing the BAN, proposed menu, equipment schedule and finish schedule. Schedule a pre-submittal meeting with DPH Environmental Health to confirm the grease interceptor size, hand sink locations and three-compartment sink requirements before final plans. Building permit fees are a percentage of construction valuation, typically $800-$15,000; DPH plan check is $828-$2,207 flat fee depending on scope.

outcomes.original: Filing step: During construction, obtain a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate (ServSafe or equivalent, $100-$250, valid 5 years) and ensure all food-handling employees complete California Food Handler training ($7-$15 per person, valid 3 years). What to say: The owner or manager must pass an ANSI-accredited food safety exam within 60 days of opening; DPH asks for the certificate at the pre-opening inspection. Every employee who handles food must complete a Food Handler course within 30 days of hire. Keep copies on site for inspection.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Before the final building inspection, schedule the Fire Department hood and suppression inspection and the DPH pre-opening inspection (at least two weeks' notice each). What to say: Contact the SFFD Bureau of Fire Prevention to inspect the commercial hood suppression system and issue the fire permit (about $446 for a restaurant under 3,000 sq ft, plus hood plan review fees). Then schedule the DPH final inspection with the plan reviewer assigned to the project, confirming hot water, hand sinks, sealed surfaces and the food safety manager certificate are ready. DPH issues the Permit to Operate (application fee $470, annual license $0 for 2026-28) after the final inspection passes.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Obtain a California Seller's Permit (free, CDTFA online) for sales tax, register as an employer with EDD (free, online) for payroll taxes, and secure workers' compensation insurance before the first employee starts. What to say: Apply for the Seller's Permit at onlineservices.cdtfa.ca.gov; it is required before opening and often requested by suppliers. Register with EDD e-Services for Business within 15 days of the first payroll; your payroll provider needs the EDD account number. Quote workers' comp insurance through a broker or State Fund (premiums are 2-6 percent of payroll for restaurant class codes); DPH and other departments may ask for proof of coverage.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 120 to 300 days. Estimated government cost: $3,100 to $15,000. Notes: This range is the time to obtain approval of the Conditional Use Authorization, the health permit and the building permit with change of use, when those approvals are granted. The 120-300 day span reflects the CUA critical path: the one comparable CUA in the Youth and Family SUD took 229 days from filing to Commission approval (April to November 2018), and typical CUA timelines including pre-application meetings, environmental review, noticing and hearing scheduling run 6-10 months. If Planning confirms in writing that the change qualifies as continuation under Section 841 instead of a new CUA, the timeline collapses to 60-120 days (the building permit and health plan check) and the $3,100 CUA fee is avoided. Government cost includes the CUA application fee (about $3,150 in 2023, CPI-adjusted from the 2023-24 schedule), building permit fees ($800-$15,000 depending on construction valuation), DPH plan check ($828-$2,207) and health permit application ($470), plus business registration ($55-$700), fire permit (about $446) and other ministerial fees. The range excludes construction costs, architect and expediter fees, and any appeal period or revision time. It is a time to approval; if the CUA is denied or the application is withdrawn, no timeline or cost is given.
